title: Milliken Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Milliken wells have a 36-foot median depth; see typical yields, water levels, drilling costs, risks and buying advice.
h1: What Milliken Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
Milliken sits on the Weld County plains, where the well record is dominated by relatively shallow wells and Denver Basin aquifer permits. Within 5 miles of town, Colorado DWR records show 2,135 permitted wells. Of those, 1,273 are recorded as constructed, while 1,332 report a total depth.

The local numbers are useful for screening a property, but they are not a guarantee for one lot. A driller still needs to review the parcel, nearby well logs, intended use, access, casing and grout requirements, and the applicable DWR permit conditions.

sections.heading: Milliken wells are usually shallow, but the range is wide
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Milliken is 36 feet. The middle half runs from 22 to 60 feet, and 95% of wells are under 100 feet. The 90th percentile is 83 feet. That is a favorable starting point when a driller prepares a bid for a typical plains property.

The record is not uniform. Wells between 100 and 300 feet make up 3% of the depth mix, and wells between 300 and 600 feet make up 2%. The deepest recorded well is 900 feet. Permits identify Denver Basin aquifers for 76% of wells, while 1,336 name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer and 354 name Alluvial aquifers. Local geology can still change the result sharply from one parcel to the next.

sections.heading: Most Milliken wells report strong production
sections.html:
Only 210 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are a smaller sample than the depth statistics. Among those reports, the median yield is 21.5 gallons per minute, and 80% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 15% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, while 4% are in the 1-to-5-gallon range. The reported middle half is unusually broad at 15.0 to 868.8 gallons per minute, which signals a dataset with very large reported values and limited comparability. A buyer should ask for the actual well test, pump information, storage capacity and intended household, livestock or irrigation use.

sections.heading: Milliken water levels are close to the surface
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are shallow. The median depth to water is 11 feet, with the middle half between 7 and 19 feet below the surface. That can reduce the lift a pump must handle, but it also means excavation, trenching and wellhead work deserve attention during wet conditions.

The decade comparison does not show a dropping water table in these records. The median measured depth to water was 16 feet in the 2010s and 10 feet in the 2020s, meaning the reported water level was closer to the surface in the newer decade. This is a permit-record trend, not a guarantee of seasonal or parcel-specific conditions. A driller should verify the static level at the property and inspect neighboring well information.

sections.heading: Milliken permit activity spans decades
sections.html:
Milliken has a long permit history. Records show 106 permits from the 1950s, 141 from the 1960s, 74 from the 1970s, 75 from the 1980s, 319 from the 1990s, 211 from the 2000s, 244 from the 2010s and 457 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026.

The most active names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 574 wells; Clement, Glenn A., with 118; and Drilling Engineers Inc. (Smith, Chester C.), with 61. These records describe historical permit activity, not a current recommendation or proof that a driller is available. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, scope of work and who will handle the permit before signing a contract.

sections.heading: A typical Milliken well has a manageable drilling bid
sections.html:
The cost model for Milliken uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock at $50 to $70 per foot. At the 36-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,800 to $2,500. That figure is only the hole, not a functioning water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,800 to $14,500 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, extra casing or unusual electrical and trenching work can move the price. Ask for a written bid separating drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, trenching, electrical and permit-related work so competing bids cover the same scope.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic setbacks, and low-use details
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information deserves a closer look before closing. The area within about 10 miles contains 1,931 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3 historic mine features and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A map point does not by itself establish contamination at a parcel, but it is a reason to order a current water test and review environmental records for the specific address.

Low yield is not the main pattern in the reported Milliken sample, yet 1,925 wells do not report a pump yield. A dry hole or weak production is still possible on an individual lot. Confirm septic suitability, well-to-septic separation, drainage, access for a rig, building envelopes and electrical routing. Household-use wells may be exempt wells, but the permit controls the allowed use; irrigation or expanded use may require different water rights or an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: Use nearby wells to price and plan your Milliken lot
sections.html:
Before buying, pull the DWR permit and construction records for the property and compare nearby wells in Johnstown, Gilcrest, Berthoud, Platteville, Evans and La Salle when the geology and aquifer are comparable. Look for total depth, casing, static water level, pump yield, water quality and the permitted use. The local median is a useful benchmark, not a promise.

For a new build, make the well, septic system, driveway and utility routes part of the site plan from the beginning. Have a licensed driller confirm the likely target and access conditions, then obtain a water-quality test before relying on the supply. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin or the proposed use goes beyond ordinary exempt household use, ask a water-rights professional whether an augmentation plan is required.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Milliken, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Milliken is 36 feet. The middle half runs from 22 to 60 feet, and 95% are under 100 feet. The deepest record is 900 feet, so a typical bid may be shallow while an individual property can differ substantially.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Milliken?
faq.a: Using the local cost model of $50 to $70 per foot, a drilled hole at the 36-foot median depth is about $1,800 to $2,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $7,800 to $14,500. Depth, access and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Milliken well produce?
faq.a: Among the 210 Milliken-area wells that report a pump yield, the median is 21.5 gallons per minute. 80% report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 4% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Because most records do not include yield, request the actual test for the property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Milliken, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit record alone. Within about 10 miles are 1,931 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, along with 3 historic mine features and 4 EPA cleanup sites. Test the specific well for relevant contaminants, review nearby environmental records and retest after well or septic work.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Milliken?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not indicate a dropping water table. Median static water level was 16 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 10 feet in the 2020s, so newer measurements were closer to the surface. This is a record-based comparison, not a guarantee for every parcel or season.
